Authorization and safety boundaries for radiation therapists vary considerably: authority to modify prescriptions, approve treatment plans, shut down malfunctioning equipment and manage patients is divided among radiation oncologists, medical physicists, therapists and other roles. No checklist can replace checking the actual authority and operating procedures of the target position.

First observe whether you can position patients precisely according to prescriptions and treatment plans, verify identity and dose at every treatment, and immediately report or stop equipment when patients have abnormal reactions. Then complete a full exercise using the fictional materials R1—R5 in the entry module: verify prescriptions and identity, record equipment and doses, and flag items requiring confirmation or escalation. The exercise requires only paper and text files, with no real patients, real equipment or license needed.

Signals worth considering include willingness to repeat positioning and dose checks under radiation protection procedures, patience with patients and accurate recording. Reasons for caution include treating standard procedures as something you can simplify at will, or changing prescriptions, doses and treatment plans without authorization. Such boundary violations can have serious consequences in radiation therapy and should be clarified before taking a job.

This card's conclusions come from public occupational task information and editorial synthesis. They are not your personal assessment results and do not predict employment outcomes. Radiation therapists' actual scope of work depends on their institution, equipment and authorization system; the same Chinese title may involve different duties and authority in different hospitals.

If you are willing to care for cancer patients over the long term under strict procedures and safety constraints, and regard accuracy and documentation at every treatment as your responsibility, this work is worth exploring. When evaluating a position, first clarify three matters: whether you can independently perform routine treatments, who can modify prescriptions and treatment plans, and to whom you escalate equipment abnormalities or adverse patient reactions.

The same person often connects several aspects of radiation therapy work, but these differ in nature: some involve positioning according to prescriptions and treatment plans, some depend on equipment and dose data, and others follow radiation protection and documentation rules. Considering them separately helps you identify which abilities a position actually requires.

entries: Positioning and treatment | Position patients precisely and deliver doses as prescribed | Position patients according to prescriptions and treatment plans, operate radiation therapy equipment to deliver prescribed doses to designated sites, and verify patient identity, treatment site and equipment parameters at every treatment.

Radiation protection | Follow protection principles for patients, yourself and others | Use shielding and monitoring devices according to protection procedures, control exposure time and distance, wear a personal dosimeter and record readings.

Equipment checks | Verify equipment operating status before and after startup | Check radiation therapy equipment and immobilization and protection devices, confirm that parameters and interlocks function properly, and take equipment out of service and report abnormalities.

Patient observation and care | Observe and reassure patients during treatment | Observe patient responses during treatment, report abnormalities to the physician or shut down equipment, and explain treatment reactions and precautions to patients and families.

Records and doses | Maintain treatment records and dose data | Record the dose, equipment settings and patient responses for every treatment, calculate or verify the dose actually delivered each time, and keep records traceable.

Planning collaboration | Assist with treatment planning and tumor localization | Assist physicians and medical physicists in preparing the physical and technical aspects of treatment plans, participate in dosimetry and tumor localization, and schedule and coordinate treatment times.

The responsibility is diagnostic imaging examinations, requiring imaging equipment operation and image quality judgment. The responsibility is dose calculation and treatment planning, requiring dosimetry, anatomy and planning system skills. Treatment delivery experience helps, but dose calculation and plan design require separate learning and usually specialized training.

More suitable for people interested in dose calculations, plan design and planning systems. Treating experience in treatment positioning as a direct qualification for dosimetry underestimates the professional entry requirements.
Collaborate with physicians and medical physicists to calculate doses and design and optimize radiation therapy plans, producing dose distributions, treatment plans and planning records.

The responsibility is radiopharmaceuticals and radionuclide imaging, requiring radionuclide handling and imaging equipment skills. Some radiation protection knowledge from radiation therapy transfers, but radiopharmaceuticals and imaging interpretation require separate learning.

More suitable for people willing to work with radionuclides and imaging who are interested in handling radiopharmaceuticals. Those highly sensitive to radionuclide safety concerns should try a small-scale practical experience before deciding.
Prepare and administer radiopharmaceuticals and operate imaging equipment, producing radionuclide images, dose records and procedure records.

The responsibility is ultrasound imaging examinations, requiring ultrasound equipment operation and real-time image interpretation. Radiation therapy experience does not transfer directly; separate training is required.

More suitable for people interested in real-time ultrasound imaging and precise operation. Treating radiation therapy experience as direct experience qualifying you for ultrasound work underestimates the training requirements.
Operate ultrasound equipment to examine patients, acquire images in real time and make preliminary interpretations, producing ultrasound images and examination records.

The responsibility is respiratory function assessment and treatment, requiring respiratory support equipment and airway management skills. Radiation therapy experience does not transfer directly; separate training and assessment are required.

More suitable for people willing to handle airway management and respiratory support who can bear emergency care pressure. Those who find acute-care situations highly draining should first try a limited experience.
Assess respiratory function and operate respiratory support and treatment equipment, producing treatment records and patient response records.
Respiratory Therapist
The responsibility is simulation and imaging before treatment, requiring CT simulation, immobilization device and image interpretation skills. This is a preparatory stage for treatment delivery.

More suitable for people interested in imaging anatomy, positioning accuracy and immobilization devices. Without taking responsibility for treatment plans and equipment parameters, long-term development may be limited.
Make immobilization devices for patients, perform CT simulation and verify images and treatment extent, producing localization images and immobilization records.

values: Materials and Scenario | All Data Are Fictional and Editorially Designed

You are a radiation therapist at the fictional Heguang Cancer Center. Review the treatment record for fictional patient T-2401 and recommend continuing treatment, deferring it or conducting a review. All materials and values below are entirely fictional, not real prescriptions, doses or patient data.

R1 Patient and prescription record: patient code T-2401, prostate cancer diagnosis, prescribed dose 2.0 Gy per treatment for 39 treatments, treatment site prostate, with daily localization verification ordered. R2 Equipment and parameter record: linear accelerator LA-03 passed the morning check; treatment couch and immobilization devices are normal. R3 Dose and settings data: treatment 12 recorded a dose of 2.0 Gy; energy and radiation field match the plan, but the plan version number is not recorded. R4 Abnormality and response record: patient reports a mild skin reaction, recorded for observation; a positioning deviation of 0.3 cm was corrected by repositioning and remeasured. R5 Review and approval section: the draft says Continue treatment, but the review field is blank.
Task

Check R1—R5 item by item and state which items match the plan, which require review or deferral, which lack sufficient information, and which unconfirmed items and approver must be included in a recommendation to continue treatment.
Do not add dose, diagnosis or authorization information absent from the scenario; list unknowns separately.
Reference Deliverables

Matches the plan: treatment 12 dose of 2.0 Gy, energy and radiation field consistent with the plan, morning equipment check passed, and immobilization devices normal. Needs review: the record lacks a plan version number; check the controlled plan version before adding it. The 0.3 cm positioning deviation was corrected by repositioning and remeasured; confirm whether it is within the institution's tolerance. For observation: the patient's skin reaction is recorded for observation; check grading criteria and decide whether to report it to the physician.

A recommendation to continue treatment must state that the plan version awaits verification and the skin reaction awaits confirmation, and must be approved by an authorized physician. The therapist only submits the recommendation.
Boundaries

This exercise involves no real patients, real prescriptions or operation of real equipment. Actual treatment, doses and responses follow the institution's procedures and authorization. If you cannot judge, you may write Insufficient basis to judge and explain what evidence is missing.
